analysis.one_liner: Requires a licensed physician to review and approve any Medicare Advantage care denial made using AI.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2026 with one Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor and was referred to two House committees, where it has sat with no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set rules for how Medicare Advantage plans — the private insurance alternative to standard Medicare — can use artificial intelligence when denying requests for prior authorization, the approval a patient must get before a service is covered. Under the bill, an insurance plan could not deny care based on an AI output unless a qualified physician in the relevant specialty personally reviewed and signed off on the denial, attesting that they exercised independent medical judgment. The plan would also have to tell the patient's doctor that AI was involved, let them speak directly with the reviewing physician, disclose the reviewer's identity, keep records for 10 years, and submit regular reports so federal health officials can audit the plans' use of AI.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Advantage enrollees whose doctors' requests for care are denied — and the doctors who fight those denials. Roughly half of Medicare beneficiaries are in Medicare Advantage plans, and investigations and reporting in recent years have documented plans using algorithms to help process large volumes of prior-authorization denials, sometimes with little or no individual physician review. The bill requires a human doctor with the right specialty, license, and board certification to actually review and approve every AI-associated denial, and gives providers the right to talk with that doctor before the denial is final.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare Advantage patients facing AI-driven denials

how_it_helps.text: An MA plan may not issue a prior-authorization denial based on AI output unless a qualified physician reviewer reviews and approves it under a plan medical director's clinical direction [S2].

The physician must sign an attestation that their medical judgment was independent of the AI output, that the denial was not generated or dictated by AI, and that any software used was for administrative purposes only [S2].

The plan must give the requesting provider the signed attestation, a chance to communicate directly with the physician reviewer, and a chance to discuss the proposed clinical basis for the denial; it must also disclose AI involvement and the reviewer's provider ID number to the patient and provider [S2].

Plans must keep records of each denial for at least 10 years and report denials made using AI output to the Secretary every 90 days, including attestations and the algorithms and decision protocols involved [S2].

The Secretary of Health and Human Services gains explicit audit authority: comparing AI outputs to actual denials, checking overturned-denial rates, reviewing policies and algorithms, and interviewing employees [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage insurance companies bear the cost: they would have to employ or contract with qualified physician reviewers in the right specialty for every AI-associated denial, produce signed attestations, maintain records for a decade, and file quarterly reports. Some added cost could ultimately pass through to premiums or plan payments, which are largely federally financed.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not ban AI-assisted denials — a plan can still deny care using an AI tool as long as a physician signs off afterward, so critics could argue it legitimizes the practice rather than ending it [S2].

Compliance adds real administrative cost for MA plans — physician reviewers, attestations, 10-year record retention, and quarterly reporting — which could feed into premiums or federal plan payments [S2].

Enforcement depends entirely on the Secretary of Health and Human Services using the new audit authority and issuing regulations within one year of enactment, so the protections are only as strong as future administrations' willingness to enforce them [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient protections are real and targeted at a documented problem: care denials processed by algorithms without meaningful human review. The main honest objection is that the bill regulates rather than prohibits AI denials, and its safeguards rely on physician attestations and federal audits that could be carried out loosely. Still, for seniors whose medically necessary care is denied at scale by software, a mandated independent physician review with disclosure and audit trails is a meaningful check at a modest administrative cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in July 2026 and sent to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, where it has had no hearings, no markup, and no floor action while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 16, 2026 by Rep. Conaway, joined by Rep. Murphy as its one cosponsor, a Republican [S1][S3][S4].
It was referred the same day to the Committee on Ways and Means and the Committee on Energy and Commerce, with a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker [S4].
No further action has been taken since the referrals [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare Advantage insurers, who remain free to issue AI-assisted prior-authorization denials without the mandated physician review, disclosure, or federal auditing the bill would impose.

for.name: Rep. Herb Conaway
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member jurisdiction overlap; lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring physician review of AI-assisted Medicare Advantage prior-authorization denials.

for.name: Rep. Gregory Murphy
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's sole cosponsor, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is bipartisan but tiny: one Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, and no member has acted against it because no committee or floor action has occurred.

industries.note: The bill requires a qualified physician to review and approve any AI-based prior-authorization denial, plus disclosure, record-keeping, quarterly reporting, and federal audit exposure. Insurers have used AI tools to help process prior-authorization denials at scale, so the requirement raises their denial-processing costs and slows a cost-control tool that reduces the care they pay for.

Doctors who submit prior-authorization requests gain the right to speak directly with the reviewing physician, see the attestation, and dispute the clinical basis for a denial before it is final. Physician reviewers in matching specialties would also be needed by plans, creating paid review work.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has one cosponsor and no committee activity — no hearing, markup, or vote — after referral to two committees, a common resting point. With the 119th Congress ending in January 2027 and Medicare Advantage rules already a heavily lobbied area, the most likely path is that the bill dies quietly in committee unless it is folded into a broader Medicare or health package; even then, its chances of floor consideration in the remaining months are slim.
